title: Outage: /var is full and the order database has stopped

lines.text: 08:52 postgres[1187]: PANIC:  could not write to file "pg_wal/xlogtemp.1187": No space left on device
09:00 shopd[2214]: ERROR database unavailable; checkout answers 500
postgres[4120]: LOG:  database system is ready to accept connections
warehouse-sync[3310]: ERROR connection to the order database refused; this morning's orders were not sent to the warehouse

objective: Diagnosing storage issues: full disks, inode exhaustion, failing drives
secondaryObjectives: Reading and interpreting system logs for root-cause analysis

sources.note: Relevant text: Troubleshooting, 'Hardware/storage: Diagnose boot, mount, and repair issues'; 'Fix SELinux, permission, and vulnerability issues'. Read on CompTIA's certification page through a summarizing fetch on 2026-11-11; the XK0-006 objectives PDF was not opened. The course objective titles are the course seed's (2026-11-07).

Relevant text: 'If the name was the last link to a file but any processes still have the file open, the file will remain in existence until the last file descriptor referring to it is closed.' Read in primary text on 2026-11-11. Why df counts space that du cannot find, and why restarting the process that holds the file frees it.

Relevant text: 'A specification of the form ``+L1'' will select open files that have been unlinked.' Read through a summarizing fetch on 2026-11-11 (the first 100,000 characters; the output column list was not reached, so the column layout shown in the scenario is an authored rendering).

Relevant text: df 'displays the amount of space available on the file system containing each file name argument'; -h 'print sizes in powers of 1024 (e.g., 1023M)'; -i 'list inode information instead of block usage'. Read through a summarizing fetch on 2026-11-11.

sources.cite: PostgreSQL 18 Documentation, 27.6.2 Disk Full Failure, and 28.5 WAL Configuration
sources.note: Relevant text (27.6.2): 'A filled data disk will not result in data corruption, but it might prevent useful activity from occurring. If the disk holding the WAL files grows full, database server panic and consequent shutdown might occur.' 'If you cannot free up additional space on the disk by deleting other things, you can move some of the database files to other file systems by making use of tablespaces.' (28.5, wal-configuration): 'after a checkpoint, WAL segments preceding the one containing the redo record are no longer needed and can be recycled or removed'; the server removes or recycles them itself. Both read in primary text on 2026-11-11. That deleting segments by hand can remove ones crash recovery still needs is the scenario's reading of 28.5, not a quoted warning; the exact PANIC wording in the scenario's journal lines is an authored rendering.

Relevant text: SystemMaxUse= and SystemKeepFree= default to 10% and 15% of the file system, 'but each of the calculated default values is capped to 4G.' Read through a summarizing fetch on 2026-11-11. Why the system journal is not what filled /var here.

brief.situation: You are the on-call Linux administrator at Fernhill Books, a fictional online bookshop. At 09:00 checkout starts answering 500. On app01, /var is a separate 20 GB file system holding PostgreSQL's data and the application logs. A colleague says that at 08:40 they deleted a huge debug log in /var/log/shopd to free space, 'so it should be fine now'. The warehouse sync job reads the order database at 09:45. Find out what is holding the space, bring the database back without losing data, and make sure it does not happen again.
handover: shopd is the shop application, a systemd service. Its log level was raised to debug yesterday for an investigation.
PostgreSQL's data directory and WAL are under /var/lib/postgresql.
howItWorks: Run commands from the command line: type one, or pick it from the suggestions or the action list. Only this lab's commands run; there is no free shell, and each command's arguments come from its list.
Each command takes operator time: run it, then let it finish, which moves the clock by the minutes it takes. The outage keeps developing on the same clock.
The map shows each host, device or service and the links between them, with a status in words. Output appears in the terminal as it happens.
When you declare the service restored, you write the incident record and explain your reasoning.

source.note: How many operator minutes each command or change takes, and when the fictional outage spreads, are teaching simplifications for exam practice, not measured values. The warehouse sync runs at 09:45, 45 minutes after the first report.

writeup.question: For the incident record: why /var stayed full after the log was deleted, how you got the space back and the database up, and what stops it happening again.

parts.label: Why the space did not come back
parts.criteria: Explains that a deleted file stays on disk while a process holds it open (unlink), which is why df and du disagree, and names lsof +L1 as how to find the holder.
parts.modelAnswer: Deleting debug.log removed only its name; shopd still had it open, so the 18 GB stayed allocated until the file was closed. df counted it, du could not see it, and lsof +L1 showed shopd holding the deleted file.

parts.label: Recovery without data loss
parts.criteria: Frees the space by restarting (or otherwise closing the file in) the holding process, reads why PostgreSQL stopped, then starts it and verifies; never deletes database files or WAL to make room.
parts.modelAnswer: I restarted shopd, which closed the file and freed 18 GB, read in the journal that PostgreSQL had stopped on a WAL write to a full disk, started it so it could recover from its WAL, and checked the health endpoint. Deleting WAL to make room would have thrown away what recovery needs.

parts.label: Prevention
parts.criteria: Turns debug logging off (and makes it take effect), and caps or rotates the application log; notes that removing a log in use should go through the application or a truncate, not rm.
parts.modelAnswer: LOG_LEVEL is back to info and took effect with the restart; the log gets rotation with a size cap. Next time, truncate a live log or rotate it through the application instead of deleting it.

expertPath.text: df shows /var at 100%; du finds only 1.3 GB, so the space is held by a deleted file that is still open.
lsof +L1 names shopd holding the deleted debug.log; journalctl shows PostgreSQL stopped on a WAL write to a full disk, not on damage.
Set LOG_LEVEL back to info, restart shopd (the space comes back and the new level takes effect), start PostgreSQL, check the health endpoint.
Record the deleted-but-open log as the cause, and a log level and rotation cap as the prevention.

restored.headline: Good: restored cleanly
restored.body: You traced the full disk to a deleted file still held open, freed it by restarting its process, let PostgreSQL recover on its own WAL and turned off what caused it.

restoredGaps.headline: Restored, with gaps
restoredGaps.body: Checkout works. The criteria show what it cost: time, a lucky guess instead of lsof, logs deleted on the way, or debug logging still on.

walLost.headline: WAL deleted
walLost.body: PostgreSQL removes old WAL itself after a checkpoint; the segments left are what it needs to recover. Free space elsewhere, here by closing the deleted log.

syncFailed.headline: The outage reached the warehouse
syncFailed.body: The database was still down at 09:45. df and du disagreeing pointed at a deleted, open file within minutes; lsof +L1 names it.

stillDown.headline: Closed too soon
stillDown.body: Checkout was still failing. Free the space, start the database and check the service before you close.

time_up.headline: Time up
time_up.body: No record was written before the run's hard limit.

scoring.modelReasoning: /var at 100% with du finding only 1.3 GB means space held by a deleted file that is still open (unlink keeps the file until the last descriptor closes). lsof +L1 names shopd holding the deleted debug.log; the journal shows PostgreSQL stopped on a WAL write to the full disk. Set the log level back to info, restart shopd so the file is closed and the level applies, start PostgreSQL so it recovers from its WAL, and verify with the health check. Never delete WAL or the logs to make room.
